# dsh-session-delete

Add a **Delete Session** action to the DeepSeek Harness (DSH)
sidebar. Choosing it permanently remov

es the Session's stored log and its projection cache, and
drops the sidebar row without a page reloa

the Session's stored log and its projection cache, and
drops the sidebar row without a page reload.

> [!IMPORTANT]
> **This project was written by AI.** The code, this README, and every other file in

this
> repository were produced by an AI coding agent (see AI authorship). It was
> reviewed and tes

ted against a real DSH install before publication, but you should treat it as
> AI-generated softwar

e: read the source before you run it, and expect rough edges outside the
> paths that were exercised

> paths that were exercised.
## Why this plugin exists
DSH has no API for deleting a Session. As of the versions this was built against:
| Candidate | What it actually does |
| `sessionController` (Host `ctx.remote.session`) | `resolveAgent` / `inspect` / `list` / `search` /
`create` / `selectModel` / `rename` / `fork` / `prompt` / `cancel` / `page` / `projections` — **no

delete** |
| `sessionPersistence` | `create` / `open` / `flush` / `stat` / `list` — an append-only l

og, **no delete** |
| `workspaceRegistry.delete(id)` | Deletes a *Workspace registration* while deli

berately retaining the directory and **every Session log** |
| `sessions` (client) | `retain` / `usi
ng` / `refreshProjections` / `search` / `fork` / `scope` / `binding` — **no delete** |

So the only way to offer the feature is to compose the official seams in the right order. This
plugi
n does exactly that, and nothing else.
## How it works

The Host half registers one loopback route, `POST /plugins/session-delete/delete`, and the browser
h
alf adds a row to each Session's `...` menu that calls it.
Deletion runs as five steps:

1. **Stop the Session** — `workspaceRegistry.archiveSession(id, { stopActivity: true })`. This is
th

e official "stop this Session's activity" path; it fans out `workspace/session-stop`, which
`dsh-age

nt`, `dsh-jobs`, `dsh-schedule` and `dsh-subagent` all listen to.
2. **Detach the live Session** — `

ctx.sessions.store.get(id).detach()`. The store keeps entries in
a non-public map, and calling the e

ntry's own `detach` is the single seam that raises
`session/disposed`.
3. **Remove the sidebar row**

— `session/disposed` → `api-session/removed`
(`dsh-api-session-controller`) → `ctx.remote.$on("api-

session/removed", …)` on the client. That
chain is the only reason the row disappears without a relo

ad.
A **cold** Session (one restored from disk that was never opened in this process) has no store
e

ntry, so `detach` cannot fire. For that case the plugin emits `api-session/removed` itself —
the sam

e signal, by the same name. Nothing on the Host listens for that event, so this is
side-effect free.

4. **Forget the membership** — `detachSession` on every Workspace, plus `unarchiveSession` and
`unp

inSession`, so no archived or pinned ghost survives.
5. **Remove the bytes** — the artifact director

y under `$DSH_HOME/sessions/<encoded-cwd>/<id>/`
and the projection cache at `$DSH_HOME/storages/ses
sion_projcache/sessions/<id>.json`.
The SQLite session index is *derived* from persistence state, so it converges on its own during the
next reconcile — the plugin does not touch it.
### What `dsh plugin add` actually does

`dsh plugin` is a thin front end for pnpm: it forwards its arguments to pnpm **inside the profile
di

rectory** (`$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/`). The part that makes the plugin load is what DSH does
ne

xt — it reconciles the profile manifest and, for every dependency that was just added and declares
a
`dsh.bundle.patch`, appends its package name to `dsh.profile.bundles`:
[代码示例省略，未执行]

`dsh.profile.bundles` is the **only** thing that decides what loads. That array is why one command
i
s sufficient and no `$DSH_HOME/cordis.patch.yml` row is required.
[该节后续省略]
## Security notes

- The route is served by the Host's web server and inherits its access policy. On DSH Desktop the
de

sktop web server rejects browser requests that its access policy denies (HTTP 403) before the
handle

r runs.
- The handler accepts only `POST`, caps the body at 64 KiB, and validates `sessionId` agains

t
`/^[A-Za-z0-9._:@-]{1,200}$/` — an id cannot escape its own directory.
- There is no authenticatio

n beyond the Host's own browser-access decision. If you expose a DSH
web server beyond loopback, und
erstand that this route deletes files.
## Limitations

- **Deletion is permanent.** There is no trash and no undo. The confirmation dialog is the only
guar

d.
- **Path shape is version-dependent.** Step 5 assumes the JSONL persistence layout
(`$DSH_HOME/se

ssions/<encoded-cwd>/<id>/` and `storages/session_projcache/sessions/`). A DSH
release that changes

either layout will need this plugin updated; step 5 would silently remove
nothing rather than fail l

oudly.
- **Non-public seam.** Step 2 reaches into `ctx.sessions.store`, which is not a public API. I

f DSH
renames or hides it, the live-Session branch degrades to the cold-Session path (which still
re

moves the bytes and the sidebar row, via step 3's explicit emit).
- **Installation needs `dsh` and p

npm.** Both ship with DSH Desktop. There is no dependency-free
install path any more — the plugin is

a profile bundle, and installing one means letting DSH
reconcile its profile manifest.
- **`remove`

can leave a dangling symlink for local-path installs.** If you installed with
`dsh plugin … add C:\

path\to\dsh-session-delete`, the profile entry is a `link:`. Removing it
prunes the manifest and the

lockfile, but the symlink at
`$DSH_HOME/profiles/<profile>/node_modules/dsh-session-delete` was obs

erved to survive; delete it
by hand. It is inert (nothing loads it), but it is untidy. Git installs

copy into the store and
are not affected.
- **`node --check` is the only automated test.** There is

no test suite. See
Testing for the manual verification that was performed.
- **Not tested on macOS o

r Linux.** The removal retry loop in `host.js` exists specifically for
Windows handle semantics. It

is written to be harmless elsewhere, but that is a reading of the
code, not a measurement.
